items.abstract: <jats:p>Prior authorization is essential to healthcare administration as a process to ensure that treatments are both clinically necessary and cost-effective prior to approval by the healthcare insurance company. In most cases, however, one or more of these data exchange and/or manual efforts coincide, increasing the burden of data management and the time needed to deliver patients' care. As HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), an innovative healthcare framework that allows electronic healthcare data to be shared and exchanged much faster and in significantly richer detail, becomes increasingly embraced, recent regulatory developments like the CMS-0057-F Final Rule and the work of artificial intelligence (AI) provide exciting new avenues to modernize prior authorization for the benefit of patients. This survey would be keen to collect and discuss the latest published research related to interoperability in healthcare (IEE) systems, FHIR format, AI-powered clinical decision support systems, explainable AI, multi-agent systems in healthcare, and the potential and benefits of using these tools to enhance the PA work process. It also identifies key areas that should be tackled regarding issues of trust, transparency, auditability, regulatory control and human oversight, and gaps in the field. Following the evidence review, the paper presents the proposed Trust-Aware Autonomous Prior Authorization Framework (TAPAF), which integrates interoperability considerations, accountabilities, governance, and AI agents to enable efficient, explainable, and patient-centric prior authorization processes.</jats:p>
title: TRUST-AWARE AUTONOMOUS PRIOR AUTHORIZATION ORCHESTRATION FRAMEWORK USING FHIR, AI, AND MULTI-AGENT HEALTHCARE SYSTEMS

items.abstract: <jats:p>Enterprise financial systems are confronted with an accelerating convergence of operational complexity, cascading service interdependencies, and regulatory compliance obligations that reactive, rule-based monitoring architectures cannot adequately address. Industry riskreporting bodies consistently document that systemically important financial institutions experience frequent critical system disruptions, with resolution under conventional, largely manual operations often extending well beyond two hours. This paper introduces MA-FSR (Multi-Agent Architecture for Financial Systems Resilience), a purpose-designed agentic AI framework comprising four cooperating specialized agents, Discovery, Root-Cause Analysis (RCA), Builder, and Runbook, coordinated over a shared episodic memory bus and governed by a probabilistic, compliance-aware orchestration layer. MA-FSR learns the joint behavioral distribution of transactional telemetry, compliance event streams, reconciliation ledger state, and infrastructure health signals through a VAE-Transformer hybrid. Agent-based discreteevent simulations over 50 enterprise nodes demonstrate: F1-Score of 0.964 against 0.912 (single-agent Transformer) and 0.734 (rule-based monitoring); AUC-ROC of 0.982; mean incident resolution time reduced from 142 to 23 minutes (84% improvement); and 41-53% of incidents autonomously resolved without human escalation, substantially exceeding industry benchmarks of 20-30%. The compliance gate mechanism achieves 100% regulatory gate adherence across all simulation runs, These simulation results indicate that MA-FSR can satisfy demanding performance and regulatory compliance-gate requirements at the same time, and they support its readiness for staged pilot evaluation in production financial infrastructure.</jats:p>
title: Agentic AI for Enterprise Systems: A Multi-agent Architecture for Financial Systems Resilience

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Purpose.&nbsp;
<div>
 A firm's multi-agent AI system approves a loan, escalates a support ticket, or rewrites a block of production code, with no human reviewing the intermediate steps. When something goes wrong, the postmortem runs into a wall: the output was the joint product of several interacting agents, none of whom made a decision in the way the organization's accountability structures expect. This paper examines why existing governance frameworks fail to answer a basic question in this setting, who is responsible, and proposes a framework that locates where that failure concentrates and why.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 Design/methodology/approach.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 This is a conceptual paper. It synthesizes the technical literature on agentic AI security, coordination, and evaluation, and extends three established organizational theories (IT governance decision-rights theory, agency theory, and sociotechnical systems theory) into the multi-agent context. The resulting framework crosses decision stakes (routine, exceptional,&nbsp;strategic) against agent architecture (single-agent, human-supervised multi-agent, autonomous multi-agent) to identify where responsibility attribution is most likely to break down.
</div>
<div>
 Findings.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 The dominant literature on agentic AI treats accountability primarily as a technical logging problem, to be solved with better audit trails and more interpretable model outputs. That is necessary but not sufficient. Responsibility attribution is fundamentally a decision-rights problem, and the highest-risk zone, exceptional and strategic decisions handled by autonomous multi-agent systems, is also the zone organizations are most eager to automate, because it is the most expensive to review with humans at scale. Three governance mechanisms follow from the framework: agent-level provenance tracking at each delegation handoff, escalation rules tied to decision type rather than model confidence, and organizational roles built specifically to interpret what the agents did.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 Practical implications.
</div>
<div>
 The framework gives compliance and internal audit functions a diagnostic for locating their own deployments on the risk grid and checking whether governance mechanisms match the risk level present. It also gives IT governance committees a vocabulary, agent authority scope, for a decision domain that current frameworks do not yet name.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 Originality/value
</div>
<div>
 Existing work on responsibility in agentic AI is either technical, focused on logging and interpretability, or normative and legal, focused on what should happen in principle. This paper extends established IT governance and decision-rights theory to the emerging context of&nbsp; enterprise multi-agent AI systems. The paper closes with a case for testing this framework against real deployments, through interviews with the people currently living inside this problem. &nbsp;
</div></jats:p>
title: Governing the Handoff: Responsibility Attribution in Enterprise Multi-Agent AI Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous AI agents executing consequential actions require authorization mechanisms that verify not only identity but voluntary intent. LICET (Latin: it is permitted) is a cryptographic middleware protocol binding AI agent authorization to real-time multi-modal physiological state via a three-layer architecture: (1) ECG waveform morphology matching as a medication-resistant identity and liveness anchor; (2) electrodermal activity (EDA) as a sympathetic cholinergic liveness signal immune to beta-adrenergic blockade; and (3) personalized Mahalanobis distance fusion over five physiological signals to elevate the cost of pharmacological coercion attacks. LICET defines a Biometric Trust Level hierarchy (L0-L3) aligned with the IETF RATS architecture (RFC 9334), per-event HKDF session-key derivation, HMAC biometric temporal signatures, Schnorr zero-knowledge proofs over BN128, and a SHA-256 hash-chained tamper-evident ledger. A reference implementation is publicly deployed at https://licet.dev/v1/.</jats:p>
title: LICET: Multi-Modal Physiological Human-Intent Verification for Autonomous AI Agent Authorization
